query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, dense Al2O3-based ceramic coating on refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) will enhance high-temperature oxygen resistance by serving as a diffusion barrier that limits oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloys in their as-manufactured state with no protective surface modification.
generation.intervention: Deposition of a uniform Al2O3-based ceramic coating (e.g., via thermal spraying or sol-gel processing) on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure at approximately 1000°C in an oxidizing atmosphere (air or pure oxygen) for durations around 100 hours, simulating extreme service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The applied Al2O3 coating forms a continuous, adherent layer that inhibits the diffusion of oxygen, slowing the oxidation kinetics of the underlying alloy.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature conditions, the Al2O3 coating develops a stable, slow-growing oxide scale that acts as a barrier against further oxygen ingress, reducing the rate of oxidation and consequent degradation of the alloy's microstructure and mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated RHEAs, the coated alloys will exhibit a lower mass gain due to oxidation, reduced oxide scale thickness, and better retention of mechanical properties after high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: Untreated RHEAs typically undergo rapid oxidation at high temperatures, leading to significant mass gain, thick and non-protective oxide scales, and a deterioration of mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This intervention is predicted to be effective up to around 1000°C under continuous oxidizing conditions; performance beyond this range or under thermal cycling remains uncertain due to risks of coating spallation or degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal coating thickness, deposition parameters, and long-term adhesion under repeated thermal cycling are not yet well established, which may affect performance.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of RHEA samples: one set with the applied Al2O3 coating and one uncoated control. Subject both sets to 1000°C in an oxidizing environment (air or oxygen) for 100 hours. Post-exposure, analyze weight changes, oxide scale formation, microstructure via SEM/TEM, and perform mechanical tests (e.g., hardness and tensile tests) to evaluate degradation.
measurements: Mass gain (difference in weight before and after exposure)
Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/TEM)
Adhesion integrity of the coating (via cross-sectional imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated RHEA samples do not display a statistically significant reduction in mass gain, thinner or more protective oxide scales, and improved mechanical property retention compared to the uncoated controls, the hypothesis is falsified.

chosen.approach: Applying protective coatings on RHEAs for oxidation resistance
